title: The engineering design process
note: Design is iterative: define the problem as measurable requirements within constraints, generate several concepts, choose by weighing trade-offs, then prototype, test, and refine. A factor of safety (failure load ÷ working load) adds margin for what you cannot know exactly.

read.title: Designing under constraints
text: Engineering starts with a need, not a solution. A team that wants a lighter wheelchair first turns the need into requirements it can test: a maximum mass, a rated load, a folded size, a target cost. Some of these are constraints, hard limits the design may not cross. Others are criteria, measures that let the team say one design is better than another.

With the problem defined, the team generates many concepts before judging any of them, then compares them, often with a weighted decision matrix. Every choice is a trade-off. Aluminum is light but less stiff than steel; carbon fiber is stiffer for its weight than either but costs far more.

Next comes a prototype, which may be cardboard on day one and machined metal a month later. Tests reveal problems, and the team loops back to change the design. That loop, not a straight line, is the engineering design process.

Because loads, material properties, and models are never known exactly, engineers add a factor of safety: the load that would cause failure divided by the load expected in use. Too little margin invites failure; too much wastes weight and money. Aircraft use about 1.5 because extra weight is so costly and their loads are studied so carefully.

q.q: In the wheelchair example, what is a constraint?
o: A hard limit the design may not cross
A concept chosen by the team

q.q: Why is the design process described as a loop?
o: Teams must buy new tools each round
Test results send the team back to change the design

q.q: Why do aircraft use a factor of safety near 1.5?
o: Weight is costly and their loads are well studied
